body.statement:
Let \(r,m\geq0\), let \(p_i\in(0,1)\) for \(1\leq i\leq r\), and let \(F_1,\ldots,F_m\) be nonzero Laurent polynomials in \(z_1,\ldots,z_r\) with nonnegative real coefficients.  If
\[
 \prod_{j=1}^m F_j(z)=c z^\gamma
 \prod_{i=1}^r\bigl((1-p_i)+p_i z_i\bigr)
\]
for \(c>0\) and \(\gamma\in\mathbb Z^r\), then there is a partition \((I_j)_{j=1}^m\) of \(\{1,\ldots,r\}\), positive constants \(c_j\), and \(\gamma_j\in\mathbb Z^r\) such that
\[
 F_j(z)=c_jz^{\gamma_j}\prod_{i\in I_j}
 \bigl((1-p_i)+p_i z_i\bigr)
\]
for every \(j\).  If every \(F_j\) has at least two monomials, then every \(I_j\) is nonempty.
body.proof_tex:
Write \(L_i(z_i)=(1-p_i)+p_i z_i\).  Multiplying each \(F_j\) by a Laurent monomial, and compensating in \(z^\gamma\), reduces to ordinary polynomials not divisible by any coordinate monomial.  We prove directly that every \(L_i\) is prime in the multivariate polynomial ring.  Regard that ring as \(A[z_i]\), where \(A\) is the real polynomial ring in the other variables.  The ring \(A\) is an integral domain because the leading monomial of a product of two nonzero polynomials has nonzero coefficient.  Division by the linear polynomial \(L_i\), whose leading coefficient \(p_i\) is a nonzero real unit, shows that
\[
 L_i\mid P \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 P\bigl(z_i=-(1-p_i)/p_i\bigr)=0.
\]
If \(L_i\mid P Q\), evaluation at that root gives a product equal to zero in the integral domain \(A\), so \(L_i\mid P\) or \(L_i\mid Q\).  Thus \(L_i\) is prime.  Two different \(L_i\)'s are not associates because they involve different variables.

Apply this prime-divisibility argument successively to the displayed product identity.  Each prime \(L_i\) divides at least one factor \(F_j\), and it cannot divide two factors because their product would then have degree at least two in \(z_i\), whereas the right side has degree one in \(z_i\) after removal of its Laurent monomial unit.  Thus each \(L_i\) divides exactly one \(F_j\).  After removing all such factors, the remaining factors multiply to a unit in the Laurent ring.  A Laurent polynomial is a unit only if it is a nonzero constant times a monomial: after shifting it to an ordinary polynomial with nonzero constant term, a product equal to one forces both factors to have degree zero in every variable.  Hence each remaining factor is \(c_jz^{\gamma_j}\), and the sets of allocated indices form the required partition.  Evaluating the identity at \(z_1=\cdots=z_r=1\) and using the nonnegative, nonzero coefficients makes every \(c_j\) positive.  Finally, a factor with \(I_j=\varnothing\) has exactly one monomial, so the last assertion follows.
